The complete sensor dataset contains approximately 800 sensor-equipped containers. However, my study focuses specifically on the urban area of Rio Maior. After spatially matching the sensor data with the GIS boundary of the study area, approximately 400 sensor-equipped containers are located within the Rio Maior urban area. 11. Are the 816 containers the full municipal park? The 816 containers represent the broader container dataset available for the municipality, including containers located both inside and outside the defined urban study area of Rio Maior. Therefore, the 816 containers should not necessarily be interpreted as the complete municipal container park. For my analysis, I use the GIS shapefile defining the boundary of the Rio Maior urban study area. Based on this boundary, only containers located within the defined study area are considered in the analysis. There are also two different sources of container information: driver-based observation records and sensor-based records. The driver-based dataset covers a larger number of containers than the sensor-based dataset. This is because sensors were installed only on a selected subset of containers as part of a pilot and testing phase. Therefore, neither the driver-based nor the sensor-based dataset should automatically be considered a complete representation of the entire municipal container network. Both provide partial coverage, with the sensor dataset being more restricted because it includes only containers equipped with sensors for experimental purposes. 12. Is glass genuinely barely instrumented (1.9 % of sensor rows vs 25 % of collection rows)? Not necessarily. The sensor dataset does not represent the full container network. Sensors were installed only on a selected subset of containers as part of a pilot and testing phase. Therefore, the fact that glass accounts for only 1.9% of the sensor records, compared with approximately 25% of the collection records, does not necessarily mean that glass containers are genuinely barely instrumented. This difference may partly reflect how containers were selected for sensor installation during the pilot phase. It is also important to distinguish between the number of records and the number of unique containers. A single sensor-equipped container can generate many records over time. Therefore, these percentages cannot be directly interpreted as the percentage of containers equipped with sensors. To determine the actual sensor coverage for glass, I would need to compare the number of unique glass containers equipped with sensors with the total number of glass containers within the defined GIS study area. Scope 17. Is Sensor-based Recyclables Collection Planning.docx the definitive scope? Is the final p-median deterministic, stochastic, or both? Yes, this document defines the current core scope of the research. However, I do not consider it a completely closed or unchangeable framework, as the methodology may be further developed as the research progresses, depending on data availability and quality. The core of the research focuses on waste-demand estimation and optimal container location. First, waste demand will be estimated using Stepwise Regression. A Deterministic Capacitated p-Median model will then be implemented as a baseline. Since waste demand is not constant in practice and is subject to uncertainty, I also intend to incorporate this uncertainty into the optimization framework. Different demand scenarios may be generated, where appropriate, using Monte Carlo Simulation and subsequently incorporated into a Stochastic Capacitated p-Median model. Therefore, both deterministic and stochastic formulations will be considered: the deterministic model will serve as the baseline, while the stochastic model will be the main formulation for addressing demand uncertainty. If appropriate, a Robust Capacitated p-Median model may also be considered as an additional benchmark. Therefore, the current core methodological framework is: Stepwise Regression → Waste-Demand Estimation → Deterministic Capacitated p-Median (Baseline) → Uncertainty/Scenario Generation→ Stochastic Capacitated p-Median (Main Model) → Robust/Sensitivity Comparison. The WSmart Route+ project studies a new paradigm on smart waste management where it explores an Engineering Systems approach, that combines data
analytics methods with Operational Research techniques to build a tool that can support decision-making in waste management systems. This tool aims to
improve waste collection operations (by increasing resources efficiency and increasing the service level provided to the citizens) supporting the adoption of a
smart waste collection based on dynamic routes as opposed to the traditional blind collection based on static routes. This project focus, as well as
methodologies fall into to the Engineering Systems scientific area since it combines engineering with perspectives from industrial management in order to
address the design and development of complex, large-scale real systems.

text: Equipa de investigação  Investigador responsável  Tânia Rodrigues Pereira Ramos Nuclear IR 40% de dedicação Ciência ID 9C1F-3BB3-36FB Instituição à qual está associado no âmbito do projeto de investigação Associação do Instituto Superior Técnico para a Investigação e o Desenvolvimento CV Obtido em 06-03-2022 at 18:40:54 GMT Sinopse do CV Tânia Ramos is an Associate Professor at the Engineering and Management Department at IST – University of Lisbon, and Vice-President of the Research Unit CEGIST. She holds a BSc degree in Management (ISCTE-IUL), a MSc degree in Operations Research and Systems Engineering (IST) and a PhD in Engineering and Management (IST). Tânia’s research focuses mainly on modelling and solving real-world problems related to logistics systems planning, routing, sustainability, reverse logistics and waste management systems. Tânia is co-author of 1 book, 8 book chapters (6 international books), and 12 peer-review articles published in indexed international journals all in Q1 from their areas of research (4 Q1: Operations Research & Management Science, 4 Q1: Engineering Environmental and Environmental Sciences according with Clarivate Analytics Web of Science and 4 Q1: Management Science and Operations Research according with SCImago Journal Ranking). The impact of Tânia’s research is acknowledged by the increasing number of citations over the years (487 citations since 2012 - the year she finished her PhD, and 107 citations in 2021), with an h-index of 9 (Scopus). Two of her most cited works are the papers entitled “Research challenges in municipal solid waste logistics management” published in Waste Management Journal in 2016 (IF 7.145), with 137 citations, and “Planning a sustainable reverse logistics system: Balancing costs with environmental and social concerns” published in Omega Journal in 2014 (IF 7.084), with 139 citations. Tânia coordinated several national projects on the fields of logistics and waste management, namely she was the PI of the FCT-Funded “WSMART Route - Waste Collection Real-Time Route Planning System” (MIT-EXPL/SUS/0132/2017) and of the ERSUC-funded project “Logistics Optimization of Selective Waste Collection using Transfer Stations”, and the Co-PI of the Open Innovation Call by Sociedade Ponto Verde-funded project “Mobile-Pro-U: Integrated system based on a mobile processing unit to recover packaging glass from undifferentiated urban waste”. Most of her papers are related to this project. The most recent ones and specifically related to the smart waste management topic are: A hybrid metaheuristic for smart waste collection problems with workload concerns (2022) 10.1016/j.cor.2021.105518 Searching for a Solution Method for the Smart Waste Collection Routing Problem (2021) 10.1007/978-3-030-85476-8_1 Dynamic Approaches to Solve the Smart Waste Collection Routing Problem (2019) 10.1007/978-3-030-10731-4_12 The smart waste collection routing problem: Alternative operational management approaches (2018) 10.1016/j.eswa.2018.03.001 Waste collection planning based on real-time information (2018) 10.1007/978-3-319-71583-4_22 Her ability to engage young researchers is also notable by the high number of thesis supervisions. Tânia supervised more than 50 Master's dissertations, 1 PhD dissertation and has 2 ongoing PhD students. TR, AP and DJ belong to CEGIST, PS and ML to INESC-ID, APA to CITTA, and HS e VG to EVOX. EVOX has expertise in the monitoring technology involved; INESC-ID has expertise in data science and machine learning techniques; CITTA excels in transportation systems and solution methods, whereas CEGIST outstands in dealing with operations management, mathematical models and waste routing problems. Additionally, the internationally recognized expert in routing problems (Daniele Vigo) will act as consultant. Finally, two waste collection companies are also involved, who represent the main beneficiaries of the project’s outcomes: 1) ERSUC currently with low maturity towards a smart collection operation (manual planning, static routes), and 2) Valorsul which already gave a small step towards a smart collection operation by installing some sensors in their waste bins, although the routes are still static. Please see the supporting letters attached. The project is grounded on multiple skills and is very multidisciplinary. Partners have worked together in the past on a one-year funded exploratory project that set the stage for the project WSmart Route+. Ana Póvoa is a Full Professor in Operations and Logistics, at the Engineering and Management Department of Instituto Superior Técnico (IST), University of Lisbon. She holds a PhD from the Imperial College of Science Technology and Medicine and her research focus is on developing a comprehensive understanding of complex problems in supply chains and operations management, supported by novel and sound engineering systems models and techniques. Sustainability, resilience, uncertainty and risk in the design and planning of supply chains are among the main research addressed domains. Ana has created and coordinates the research group in Operations Management and Logistics (OpLog) at CEGIST. Her research has led to several national and international awards having received recently the honour of being considered the best researcher in Industrial Management at the University of Lisbon. Diana Jorge is an Assistant Professor of Industrial Engineering and Management at the U. Lusofona. Diana holds a PhD in Transportation Systems from the U. Coimbra. Her research focuses mainly on modelling and solving real-world problems related to transportation and logistics systems, e.g. waste collection routing, through Operations Research methods. Diana is co-author of 8 peer-review articles published in indexed international journals with 561 citations (122 citations and an h-index of 6 in 2021) in Scopus, and participated in 3 research projects. Pedro Santos has a PhD in Mathematics from the Technische Universität Chemnitz, and Habilitation in Mathematics. He is Associate Professor at both the Mathematics and the Computer Science Departments of IST. His main academic interests are in Functional Analysis, Artificial Intelligence, and Game Design, having focused in the last years on Machine Learning and its applications to several domains. He has co-authored 3 books and has 80 publications and 190 citations registered on Publons, and more than 700 citations and h-index 15 on Google Scholar. Manuel Lopes is an Associate Professor in Computer Science and Engineering at IST. He did his PhD in Electrical and Computer Engineering in the field of machine learning and intelligent machines. text: Plano de trabalho  Resumo Resumo em português O projeto WSmart Route+ estuda um novo paradigma na gestão inteligente de resíduos. A análise de dados combinada com a otimização de rotas é explorada neste projeto para melhorar a operação de recolha de resíduos, apoiando a implementação de uma recolha inteligente baseada em rotas dinâmicas, em oposição à tradicional recolha cega baseada em rotas estáticas. Todos os dias toneladas de resíduos são recolhidas e, para tal, milhares de quilómetros são percorridos. Porém, existe uma elevada incerteza sobre a quantidade de resíduos nos contentores, facto que pode levar a uma operação ineficiente, na qual os recursos são usados para recolher uma pequena quantidade de resíduos. A título de exemplo, dados recolhidos junto do nosso parceiro ERSUC, uma das maiores empresas de recolha de resíduos recicláveis , mostram que nos municípios rurais 52% dos contentores de resíduos recicláveis foram recolhidos com um nível de enchimento inferior a 25% e apenas 9% com um nível de enchimento superior75%. Além disso, as empresas de resíduos frequentemente recebem reclamações relatando transbordos ou resíduos em redor dos contentores que prejudicam a saúde pública. Este é um caso frequente em municípios urbanos, onde um grande número de transbordos é relatado. Estes dados representam um uso ineficiente de recursos nas áreas rurais e problemas de saúde pública em áreas urbanas. Esta é uma situação comum em sistemas de gestão de resíduos. Para aumentar a eficiência e simultaneamente o nível de serviço prestado aos cidadãos serão exploradas três grandes linhas de investigação. A primeira foca na redução da incerteza em relação à procura (quantidade de resíduos em cada contentor). Para lidar com esse desafio, são exploradas três formas possíveis de aquisição de dados. Uma é a instalação de sensores, onde são feitas medições precisas dos níveis de enchimento, proporcionando um conhecimento a priori desses níveis. Mas como os sensores não são baratos e podem exigir um elevado investimento das empresas de resíduos, é explorado um segundo caminho que se baseia nas observações dos motoristas sobre os níveis de enchimento dos contentores antes de esvaziá-los. Esses dados podem ser usados para alimentar modelos de previsão robustos para prever os níveis de enchimento futuros. Esta abordagem tem um custo insignificante, mas é suscetível a erros humanos e são registadas poucas observações em comparação com a instalação de sensores nos contentores. Para ultrapassar o erro humano das observações dos motoristas, um terceiro caminho é explorado, onde uma nova abordagem de monitorização é proposta – o uso de sensores móveis pelos motoristas para medir com precisão os níveis de enchimento antes de esvaziar os contentores. Isso implica apenas um sensor (móvel) por motorista, mas poucas observações são registadas em comparação com o uso de sensor estático instalado nos contentores. Os modelos de previsão robustos são também necessários nesta abordagem. No entanto, o acesso aos dados (e tratamento) não é suficiente para aumentar a eficiência das operações nem evitar transbordos. Surge, então, a segunda linha de investigação, em que é necessário otimizar as rotas de recolha em função desses dados. A terceira linha foca-se no desafio de identificar quais os contentores que devem ter um sensor estático instalado. Uma rede completa sensorizada implica um elevado investimento dado os milhares de contentores que uma rede opera, por isso este projeto explora a escolha de um número limitado de contentores para ter sensores estáticos. Neste contexto, este projeto visa desenvolver e testar uma ferramenta para prever níveis de enchimento tendo em conta a informação dos sensores estáticos ou móveis ou dos motoristas e definir rotas ótimas de forma dinâmica, resultando em conhecimento científico inovador e benefícios práticos para a sociedade em termos de ferramenta utilizável. O WSmart Route+ tem, então, os seguintes objetivos de investigação: 1. Estudar diferentes formas de adquirir e tratar dados sobre o nível de enchimento de forma a reduzir a incerteza associada; 2. Neste contexto, este projeto visa desenvolver e testar uma ferramenta para prever níveis de enchimento tendo em conta a informação dos sensores estáticos ou móveis ou dos motoristas e definir rotas ótimas de forma dinâmica, resultando em conhecimento científico inovador e benefícios práticos para a sociedade em termos de ferramenta utilizável. O WSmart Route+ tem, então, os seguintes objetivos de investigação: 1. Estudar diferentes formas de adquirir e tratar dados sobre o nível de enchimento de forma a reduzir a incerteza associada; 2. Desenvolver e testar uma ferramenta de planeamento que combina métodos inovadores para lidar com a complexidade relacionada com a definição de rotas de recolha inteligentes, considerando dados fornecidos pelos sensores (estáticos e móveis) e pelas observações visuais dos motoristas; 3. Desenvolver modelos inovadores para decidir em quais contentores devem ser instalados sensores; 4. Desenvolver uma análise de custo-benefício comparando a situação atual com a situação futura em casos reais; 5. Desenvolver um teste-piloto em ambiente real. Estes objetivos contribuem para aumentar a eficiência dos recursos (ODS9), reduzir o impacte ambiental da atividade de recolha de resíduos (ODS11) e diminuir o número de transbordos, melhorando a gestão do saneamento básico (ODS6). Baseado na experiência da equipa [Ram1,Mor,Jor] estima-se que a ferramenta irá reduzir os custos em 30% e aumentar o nível de serviço à população. Resumo em inglês The WSmart Route+ project studies a new paradigm on smart waste management. Data analytics combined with route optimization will be explored to improve waste collection operation supporting the adoption of a smart waste collection based on dynamic routes as opposed to the traditional blind collection that is based on static routes. Everyday thousands of kilometres are travelled to collect tonnes of waste with high uncertainty on the amount of waste in each bin, a fact that can lead to inefficient collection operations where resources are used to collect o�en a small amount of waste. For instance, data gathered from ERSUC, one of the major recyclable waste collection companies operating in Portugal, showed that in rural municipalities 52% of the recyclable waste bins were collected with a fill level lower than 25% and only 9% with a fill level greater than 75%. On the other hand, waste companies o�en receive complaints reporting overflows or waste surrounding the containers which damage public health. This is o�en the case in urban municipalities, where a vast number of overflows are reported. Such facts represent inefficient resource usage in rural areas and public health issues in urban areas, a common situation in waste management systems. To increase efficiency and simultaneously the level of service provided to citizens three main research lines will be explored: The first one focus on reducing the uncertainty regarding demand (waste inside each individual bin). To deal with this challenge, three possible ways of acquiring data are explored. One is the installation of static sensors in bins, where accurate fill levels measurements are done, providing a priori knowledge of the fill levels. But as sensors are not cheap and may require a high investment from waste companies, a second path is explored that relies on visual observations from drivers on the bin’s fill levels before emptying them. The data collected should then be used to feed robust models for predicting fill levels. This approach has a negligible cost but is susceptible to human error and few observations are recorded compared to sensor in bins. To overcome the human error from the visual observation, a third path is pursued where a new monitoring approach is proposed – the use by truck collection drivers of mobile sensors to accurately measure fill levels before emptying the bins. This only implies one (mobile) sensor per truck, but few observations are recorded compared to the use of static sensor installed in bins. Also, robust predictive models are needed in this approach. 10/31 | Plano de trabalho  | |---|

Todos os dias toneladas de resíduos são recolhidas e, para tal, milhares de quilómetros são percorridos. Porém, existe uma elevada incerteza sobre a quantidade de resíduos nos contentores, facto que pode levar a uma operação ineficiente, na qual os recursos são usados para recolher uma pequena quantidade de resíduos. A título de exemplo, dados recolhidos junto do nosso parceiro ERSUC, uma das maiores empresas de recolha de resíduos recicláveis , mostram que nos municípios rurais 52% dos contentores de resíduos recicláveis foram recolhidos com um nível de enchimento inferior a 25% e apenas 9% com um nível de enchimento superior75%. Além disso, as empresas de resíduos frequentemente recebem reclamações relatando transbordos ou resíduos em redor dos contentores que prejudicam a saúde pública. Este é um caso frequente em municípios urbanos, onde um grande número de transbordos é relatado. Estes dados representam um uso ineficiente de recursos nas áreas rurais e problemas de saúde pública em áreas urbanas. Esta é uma situação comum em sistemas de gestão de resíduos. Para aumentar a eficiência e simultaneamente o nível de serviço prestado aos cidadãos serão exploradas três grandes linhas de investigação. A primeira foca na redução da incerteza em relação à procura (quantidade de resíduos em cada contentor). Para lidar com esse desafio, são exploradas três formas possíveis de aquisição de dados. Uma é a instalação de sensores, onde são feitas medições precisas dos níveis de enchimento, proporcionando um conhecimento a priori desses níveis. Mas como os sensores não são baratos e podem exigir um elevado investimento das empresas de resíduos, é explorado um segundo caminho que se baseia nas observações dos motoristas sobre os níveis de enchimento dos contentores antes de esvaziá-los. Esses dados podem ser usados para alimentar modelos de previsão robustos para prever os níveis de enchimento futuros. Desenvolver e testar uma ferramenta de planeamento que combina métodos inovadores para lidar com a complexidade relacionada com a definição de rotas de recolha inteligentes, considerando dados fornecidos pelos sensores (estáticos e móveis) e pelas observações visuais dos motoristas; 3. Desenvolver modelos inovadores para decidir em quais contentores devem ser instalados sensores; 4. Estes objetivos contribuem para aumentar a eficiência dos recursos (ODS9), reduzir o impacte ambiental da atividade de recolha de resíduos (ODS11) e diminuir o número de transbordos, melhorando a gestão do saneamento básico (ODS6). text: Accessing and treating data is not however sufficient to increase operations efficiency nor avoid overflows. Then, the second research line emerges where the focus relies on optimizing collection routes accordingly with the data collected and treated. The third research line focus on the challenge of identifying the key bins to have static sensor installed. A full sensorized network imply a high investment given the thousands of bins own by waste management systems, therefore choosing a limited number of bins to have static sensors is explored, towards a system where some bins are monitored through static sensors, some by mobile sensors, and some by visual observations. In such context, this project aims to develop and test a tool to predict fill-levels given the information from static sensors or mobile sensors or drivers and define optimal routes in a dynamic way, delivering both innovative scientific knowledge about data-driven optimization and practical benefits to society in terms of a workable tool. The ultimate goal of this project is to increase resources efficiency and improve service levels of waste management systems contributing to a sustainable development. The following research goals are then set to the present project: 1. Study different ways of acquiring and treat waste bin fill-level data to reduce associated uncertainty; 2. Develop and test a planning tool combining innovative methods to deal with the complexity related with the definition of smart collection routes, considering data provided by sensors (static and mobile) and by driver’s visual observations; 3. Develop innovative models to decide in which containers static sensors should be installed; 4. Develop a cost-benefit analysis comparing the as-is to the to-be in real case studies; 5. Develop a testbed in a real environment. The project’s objectives contribute to increase resource efficiency (SDG 9), reduce environmental impact of the waste collection activity (SDG 11), and decrease the number of overflowing bins/waste surrounding the bins, improving sanitation management (SDG 6). Instead, they usually rely on pre-planned routes travelled at regular intervals, o�en designed manually, regardless of the demand [1]. This leads to routes that are far from optimal and do not adjust to demand changes [Ram1]. Studies have shown that as regions become more developed and consumer expenditure increases, so does waste generation [2,3,4]. To address this upgrade and overcome inefficiency in waste collection, two research avenues are apparent: 1) The installation of smart sensors in bins [5,6,7] to access real-time information on bins’ fill levels that allows waste collection companies to: i) save operational costs by reducing unnecessary trips; ii) increase the quality of service to citizens, by issuing a warning when a bin is close to overflowing. We argue that a minimum fill level limit is not a good strategy to trigger a collection [Ram1] as containers with low filling levels can “be worth it” to be collected. Some companies have their driver’s recording bin fill levels every time a bin is visited. Yet, the accuracy of this information is questionable, as it has lower precision and may be prone to individual subjectivity and human error. Moreover, if fill levels are only recorded when visited, time interval between observations can be considerable, especially for recyclable waste. We introduced the Smart Waste Collection Routing Problem (SWCRP) [Ram1]. SWCRP characterizes dynamic smart routes where each day only the “best” bins to visit and the “best” visiting sequence is defined by accessing real-time information on the bins’ fill-levels through sensors and a mathematical model to maximize the daily profit (the difference between the revenues related with the weight collected and the transportation costs) while considering the problem constraints (vehicle and bins capacity, etc.). The SWCRP was modeled and solved in [Ram1] as a Vehicle Routing Problem with Profits (VRPP), an approach revealed to be myopic, that highlighted the need for a larger planning period [Mor]. We then approached the SWCRP problem as an Inventory Routing Problem (IRP) [Mor], where profit was maximized for a planning horizon of 10 days, instead of for a single day (as in VRPP). Our IRP model considers waste bins’ future fill levels in the whole planning horizon. As such, average rates from historical data through simple statistics were used. By using small-size instances, we concluded that IRP models enable better results than the VRPP model, and, therefore, we will explore IRP models in this research project. This is also corroborated by [12]. As IRP integrates inventory management with routing problems over a given time horizon [13], it addresses three different decisions: when to visit a client; how much to deliver/collect; and how to combine clients in a route [14]. When considering demand information, [15] classified the IRPs into three groups: deterministic, stochastic, and dynamic. text: identified [14] and [16]. When coupling these models with real-time information, several difficulties arise as the dynamism required to deal with updated everyday information is not straightforward. However, nowadays DIRP approaches are needed to explore access to real-time information and better support the operations’ decision-making processes. Such works are not easily found in the literature applied to waste collection having been published only two works on this subject to the best of our knowledge [17, and Mor, from our team]. We identified several gaps in the literature. Although there is a rich body of research on bin sensor systems, authors rarely contemplate alternative monitoring approaches beyond the current situation (no monitoring) and a completely sensorized network of bins. Complete sensorization is presently an unrealistic expectation due to the large investment cost and there is a lack of work to identify the optimal placement of sensors (on the bins) to minimize uncertainty. Moreover, mobile sensors or observations of the drivers were never addressed. On the other hand, there is a growing body of literature addressing predictive models for waste generation. Still, more work is needed, especially regarding day-to-day predictions on individual bins highlighting the need for i) the development of more sophisticated solutions and ii) validation of existing solutions on larger and real scales. Up to today, only a few works published explore DIRP approaches within waste collection and none of the analyzed works explored the use of predictive methods to estimate future waste bins’ fill-levels. In the published models, cost minimization is typically assumed and no concern on the profit maximization (a metric that combines the weight collected and the travelled cost) is pursued. Additionally, none of the analyzed works explored the updating of new real-time information when this becomes available. In the WSmart Route+ these gaps will be explored. The WSmart Route+ aims to increase Waste Management Systems resources efficiency and service levels provided to the citizens contributing to a more Sustainable Development. WSmart Route+ explores three main research streams: 1. The identification of the more adequate form of acquiring data from waste bins considering accuracy versus investment, and how to make predictions based on these data; 2. The usage of collected data as input to optimization models that will allow the definition of optimised operational approaches to collect waste while reducing costs and guaranteeing the communities service levels; 3. Which bins need to have more continuous monitoring to assure higher benefit/cost value. To identify the more adequate form of acquiring data from waste bins considering accuracy versus investment, and how to make predictions based on these data, we will study three different monitoring waste bins methods to reduce the uncertainty associated with their fill levels: i) Static sensors installed inside waste bins, that allow the collection of more and accurate data but imply a high investment; ii) visual observations from the truck collection drivers which are less frequent, with lower accuracy, but have a negligible cost; iii) Mobile sensors that represent an innovative solution (to the best of our knowledge) that balances the advantages and disadvantages of the other two, giving the accuracy and precision of sensor observations at a fraction of the cost. Regardless of the source data, machine learning models will be used to properly treat data and make predictions. But, collecting and treating data is not enough to increase efficiency and service level in waste management systems. It is necessary to plan the collection operation taken into account these data. Some IT companies are already exploring the use of static sensors coupled with tools to define routes, a fact revealing the relevance and importance of this problem. However, they typically use algorithms to first select a set of bins to visit based on the current or estimated fill- levels, and then run a Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) or VRP algorithm to define the collection routes. Yet, several important aspects are missing in this approach, as knowing the waste amount at each bin does not necessarily mean that only full containers should be collected on a specific day, as maybe considering small additional distances may reveal more profitable situations (e.g. collect not full containers located nearby a full container); the service level provided to the population must be considered, and defining the more “profitable” route for a day does not mean maximizing profit for a time horizon (as a decision of today o�en has repercussions on the following days). Regarding the visual observations, an ongoing practice at waste management companies, i.e., they ask the drivers to record the fill-levels before emptying a bin (typically, using a 25%-level scale). However, that information is not currently being used by the companies to optimize the collection operation. This is something that we will explore too. Finally, for the development of smart cities, with effective and low-cost waste management services, it is important to understand - given the large number of bins managed by waste management companies - which bins should have a more continuous monitoring to assure higher benefit/cost value. However, choosing which bins should be sensorized through static sensors to minimize uncertainty or provide the most relevant information is not straightforward and it is seldom studied in the literature. We will contribute to fill this gap. WSmart Route+ aims to develop a smart route planning tool and assess its benefits by answering the following open questions: 1. Data: What data sources should be used to improve efficiency and service level in waste collection operation? What is the value of information from the data collected currently by the drivers? And what would be the impact of improving the accuracy of these data by replacing visual observations by mobile sensors readings? And what would be the impact of having continuous readings (from static sensors) versus less frequent readings (from the drivers)? 2. Planning Dynamic Routes: What are the most suitable models to deal with dynamic routes? What should be the time horizon to consider? How to deal with the uncertainty when planning for the days ahead? 3. Sensor Placement: What are the waste bins that are worth being sensorized through static sensors? What are the criteria and thresholds involved in that decision? How the collection routes must be designed for collecting the non-monitored and monitored waste bins? 4. Tool: What are the most suitable algorithms capable to deliver solutions for dynamic collection routes in a short computational time? How should the data be captured - by either drivers and sensors (static or mobile), and the solution plan presented to the decision-maker? 5. Benefits: What are the benefits of using a system with the previous features when compared to the current situation? This represents tonnes of waste that need to be collected everyday through thousands of kilometers travelled and emissions of Greenhouse Gases. The high uncertainty on the waste amount in each bin can lead to inefficient collection operations where resources are used to collect o�en a small amount of waste. The WSmart Route+ aims to increase Waste Management Systems resources efficiency and service levels provided to the citizens contributing to a more Sustainable Development. WSmart Route+ explores three main research streams: 1. The identification of the more adequate form of acquiring data from waste bins considering accuracy versus investment, and how to make predictions based on these data; 2. The usage of collected data as input to optimization models that will allow the definition of optimised operational approaches to collect waste while reducing costs and guaranteeing the communities service levels; 3. Which bins need to have more continuous monitoring to assure higher benefit/cost value. text: how to make predictions based on these data; 2. The usage of collected data as input to optimization models that will allow the definition of optimised operational approaches to collect waste while reducing costs and guaranteeing the communities service levels; 3. Which bins need to have more continuous monitoring to assure higher benefit/cost value. To identify the more adequate form of acquiring data from waste bins considering accuracy versus investment, and how to make predictions based on these data, we will study three different monitoring waste bins methods to reduce the uncertainty associated with their fill levels: i) Static sensors installed inside waste bins, that allow the collection of more and accurate data but imply a high investment; ii) visual observations from the truck collection drivers which are less frequent, with lower accuracy, but have a negligible cost; iii) Mobile sensors that represent an innovative solution (to the best of our knowledge) that balances the advantages and disadvantages of the other two, giving the accuracy and precision of sensor observations at a fraction of the cost. Regardless of the source data, machine learning models will be used to properly treat data and make predictions. But, collecting and treating data is not enough to increase efficiency and service level in waste management systems. It is necessary to plan the collection operation taken into account these data. Some IT companies are already exploring the use of static sensors coupled with tools to define routes, a fact revealing the relevance and importance of this problem. However, they typically use algorithms to first select a set of bins to visit based on the current or estimated fill- levels, and then run a Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) or VRP algorithm to define the collection routes. Yet, several important aspects are missing in this approach, as knowing the waste amount at each bin does not necessarily mean that only full containers should be collected on a specific day, as maybe considering small additional distances may reveal more profitable situations (e.g. collect not full containers located nearby a full container); the service level provided to the population must be considered, and defining the more “profitable” route for a day does not mean maximizing profit for a time horizon (as a decision of today o�en has repercussions on the following days). Regarding the visual observations, an ongoing practice at waste management companies, i.e., they ask the drivers to record the fill-levels before emptying a bin (typically, using a 25%-level scale). However, that information is not currently being used by the companies to optimize the collection operation. This is something that we will explore too. Finally, for the development of smart cities, with effective and low-cost waste management services, it is important to understand - given the large number of bins managed by waste management companies - which bins should have a more continuous monitoring to assure higher benefit/cost value. However, choosing which bins should be sensorized through static sensors to minimize uncertainty or provide the most relevant information is not straightforward and it is seldom studied in the literature. We will contribute to fill this gap. WSmart Route+ aims to develop a smart route planning tool and assess its benefits by answering the following open questions: 1. Data: What data sources should be used to improve efficiency and service level in waste collection operation? What is the value of information from the data collected currently by the drivers? And what would be the impact of improving the accuracy of these data by replacing visual observations by mobile sensors readings? And what would be the impact of having continuous readings (from static sensors) versus less frequent readings (from | |---| | the drivers)? 2. Planning Dynamic Routes: What are the most suitable models to deal with dynamic routes? What should be the time horizon to consider? How to deal with the uncertainty when planning for the days ahead? 3.

text: Task 1-Data Analytics and Predictive Models (month 1 to 12). To answer the Data open question, we will use 2 datasets already available. The ERSUC and Valorsul drivers register fill levels of the individual waste bins before collecting. And data from static sensors readings obtained from 650 volumetric sensors already installed by Valorsul. A third dataset obtained through the mobile sensors readings will be created. For that, an experiment will be conducted in the first 6 months of the project where a set of drivers will be involved to collect the data with the fill-levels through mobile sensors. The three data sets will be then analysed through proper data analytics methods and data will be transformed into valuable information for management purposes (e.g., waste bin visits that could be avoided, overflows that could be avoided, etc.). The three data sets will also act as historical data to feed machine learning algorithms to help predicting future fill levels of individual bins. These predictive models are needed to plan dynamic routes with a “look-ahead perspective” in T2. Tasks 2-Smart Waste Collection Routing Problem Modelling (m 1 to 21).To answer the Planning Dynamic Routes open questions, we will explore Dynamic and Stochastic IRP with Profits models. It was concluded from the literature that smart routes demand for larger planning periods so the SWCRP should be model as an IRP with Profits, where a larger time horizon will be considered, and the accumulation of weight inside the bins are considered according to the estimates done by the prediction models from T1. The uncertainty inherent to consider days-ahead and the dynamism required in this kind of problem will be tackled in this task. All these features must be modelled, where new mathematical models will be developed. Task 3-Decision Supporting Tool for the Smart Waste Collection Routing Problem (m 7 to 27). To answer to the Tool open questions, we will design a fast and effective solution method based on meta-heuristics to solve the models developed in T2. Then, from an information management perspective, the requirements from the waste collection companies on which information they need, when and in which format will be gathered through meetings and interviews with waste collection companies’ operations managers, to develop a prototype of a Graphic User Interface. Task 4-Strategic Location for Sensors Placement (m 13 to 24). To answer to the Sensor Placement open question, we will explore the criteria that influences the decision of sensorizing or not a waste bin and embed those criteria in a decision model to support the decision of which containers should be monitored with static sensors. Having a full sensorized network, where companies typically owned thousands of bins and sensors are still expensive, is very difficult to implement. Moreover, the value of the information transmitted by the sensors will be higher in some waste bins (e.g., more remote bins, with high variability) and lower in others (e.g., non-remote bins with a stable filling rate). Then, not all waste bins in a network are worth to be monitored with a static sensor. Task 5 - Cost-Benefit Analysis (m 22 to 30). To answer to the Benefits open question, a cost-benefit analysis will be conducted to evaluate the potential market value of this research project. For that, we will test the smart route planning tool with real data (from ERSUC and Valorsul) and assess the benefits of using a system like this when comparing it to the current situation, i.e., blind collection with pre-defined collection frequencies. Historical data from the waste collection companies analysed at T1 will now be used to generate a simulation environment to test four scenarios. Task 6-Prototype Tool Validation (m 28 to 36). Finally, and to validate the tool developed in a real environment, a testbed will be conducted at ERSUC. text: Pessoas / Mês Alocados 12 BI-a - 02 Bolsa de Investigação - Estud. dout. ou lic. e mestres em CNCG Instituto de Engenharia de Sistemas e Computadores, Investigação e Desenvolvimento em Lisboa 1.8 Manuel Lopes Instituto de Engenharia de Sistemas e Computadores, Investigação e Desenvolvimento em Lisboa 3 Pedro Alexandre Simões dos Santos Instituto de Engenharia de Sistemas e Computadores, Investigação e Desenvolvimento em Lisboa Descrição Task 1 aims to evaluate different data acquisition methods and treat waste bin fill-level data to reduce associated uncertainty. In this set, three sources of data are considered: 1) drivers records (from the two engaged companies – ERSUC and Valorsul); 2) static sensors readings (from Valorsul), and 3) mobile sensors readings. Regarding drivers’ records, both companies have already these data and will make them available for this project. Regarding static sensors readings, the sensors used are volumetric sensors developed by our partner Evox Technologies, that uses ultrasonic technology and encompass a communication unit and a battery. They measure, communicate and detect events related with the waste container's volume. Since 650 static sensors were installed since 2020 at Valorsul, there is also a huge amount of data available. Regarding the new monitoring method – mobile sensors, no available data exist (since it is new and aimed to be studied further in this project). To collect these data, an experiment will be conducted for 6 months, where a set of drivers will be involved and they will use the mobile sensors every time they visit a bin, besides doing the visual observation. For this experiment, the sensors from Evox will be used, but in a mobile version, i.e., without being fixed/installed. We will use the same bins that have already static sensors installed (from Valorsul), and thus we will be able to have different data (static sensor readings, mobile sensor readings and visual observations) for the same waste bins, and for the same period of time (6 months). This will allow to compare the three data sets, using statistical methods, and able to draw some conclusions. Besides the comparison between the three data sets, we will perform predictions based on each one of them. For that, data analytics techniques will be applied, ranging from simple temporal series modelling [19], to more complex methods that can be used when more information is available [20]. Models based on LSTM neural networks [Cos] can exploit information about each location, e.g. type of neighbourhood, commercial or residential, day of the week, holidays vs. school days, and others. Then, predictive models will be adjusted to estimate future fill levels for each bin. To validate the predictive models, each source set (drivers records, static sensors readings and mobile sensors readings) will be split into a training set and a testing set, allowing the predictive models to be trained with the data from the training set, and applied to give estimates for the testing set. The ultimate goal of this task is to compare how good are the estimates done by each source of data and conclude on the value of information given (e.g., waste bin visits that could be avoided, overflows that could be avoided, etc.)., when proper data analytics and predictive methods are applied. Task 1 will be mainly performed by INESC-ID team, expert in machine learning techniques. EVOX team will also support this task regarding the sensor data set. It was modelled and solved as a Vehicle Routing Problem with Profits (VRPP), which implies a planning horizon of just one day. Given the feedback from the industry along the previous project, and also based on the literature [Mor1], it was concluded that the planning period should be larger than one day. To consider wider planning horizons the problem should be modelled as an Inventory Routing Problem (IRP), where the (estimated) inventory levels for each waste bin, for each day of the planning period are taken into account, coupled with the routing decisions. Therefore, IRP models are deepen explored in this project as firstly as deterministic, being later extended to deal with uncertainty: 1. Deterministic IRPs assume that demand information is known by the decision-maker at the beginning of the planning horizon. The deterministic IRP model proposed by [Mor1] will be deepen in this task. 2. Stochastic IRPs (SIRP) explore data characteristics; data analytics (Task 1) will be used to extract such characteristics from historical data. Uncertainty modelling techniques will be then applied to solve the SIRP. In particular, stochastic or robust optimization will be studied. 3. Dynamic IRPs (DIRP) assume that demand is not completely known at the beginning of the planning horizon but that it will be gradually revealed over time. This characteristic is of special interest to this project, since using real-time information from the sensors naturally enables a “dynamic” context. Dynamic stochastic approaches are then explored, and the work developed previously will be extended to deal with the dynamic nature of the problem considering the uncertain context. In the previous works [Ram1, Mor1], the objective function considered was Profit Maximization (revenues from selling the recyclable waste minus the transportation cost related to the waste collection). Nevertheless, and from the feedback from practitioners, it became clear that the service level to the population must also be a priority (service level can be measured by the number of overflowing bins and/or imposing a maximum time without visiting a waste bin, that impact public health issues and must be accounted for). Therefore, in this task, this objective will be also considered. Different ways of addressing this objective will be explored: 1) multi-objective approaches [21], where two objectives are at stake – maximize profit and minimize overflows ; 2) maintain a single objective approach but including a cost that represents the service level (in other words, include the cost of overflow). Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) models will be developed along points 1) to 3) and different types of formulations will be implemented and tested. The MILP models will be implemented with GAMS language and solved through the CPLEX Optimizer. To test the models, test instances from the previous exploratory research project will be used and also new ones will be generated using the data collected at Task 1 to better represent real waste collection problems. This task will be mainly performed by CEGIST team, given their knowledge in modelling routing problems. A dynamic route scenario demands for short computational times. Moreover, since this research project intends to produce some knowledge to be transfer to practitioners (through the development of a prototype of a decision support tool to plan smart collection routes), large size problems will be at stake, and the prototype must be developed under a programming language that can be used by companies. Therefore, this task has two goals: develop metaheuristics to solve the IRP and develop a Graphic User Interface prototype for the Decision Supporting Tool, where the metaheuristics developed plus the predictive methods from Task 1 are embedded. Knowing that routing problems are typically very complex to solve, the problems addressed at Task 2 (Deterministic IRP, Stochastic IRP and Dynamic IRP) will now be solved using heuristics and meta-heuristics [Jor], techniques that have proved to provide good solutions in short period of time within traditional routing problems. Apart from the solution’s time enhancement, is important to prove that the solution method is able to find good solutions (optimal or near-optimal solution). To that end, the test instances devised at Task 2 will be use at Task 3. The solutions obtained will be compared to the results from Task 2 in order to assess how close the heuristic solutions are from the optimal solution. In that way, the effectiveness of the solution approach is tested. Then, the solution methods developed in this task, plus the predictive methods developed at Task 1 (either for the drivers records historical data and sensors readings historical data) will be embedded in a prototype for the Graphic User Interface (GUI) for the Decision Supporting Tool to plan smart collection routes. Although monitoring technologies, as volumetric sensors, allow to better understand these systems and to gain insights from the data collected, they are still very pricey. It is then necessary to develop financially more sustainable strategies for integrating sensors into the waste collection activities. For that, in this task, it will be analysed in which circumstances makes sense to have a static sensor embedded in a container to measure its fill level. A set of criteria will be identified taking into account the characteristics of the containers and their relevance for the problem (e.g. location, type of population and facilities nearby, level of predictability, etc.). A decision support model will be proposed, and it must be such that it helps minimizing the investment costs associated with the utilization of the volumetric sensor technology (by monitoring only a reduced number of containers) while maintaining the benefits inherent to its use. Thus, a trade-off analysis between the cost and benefits of monitoring all the containers or only few of them will be performed in order to comprehend the feasibility of the proposed decision support model. The model will select from a full set of containers which of those containers must have their fill level measured in real time through the use of volumetric sensors. In the first strategy, criteria like average fill rate, variance, remoteness, etc., of each container will be considered to select containers through sampling techniques. Then, in the second step, routes will be defined following two approaches: 1) using the predictive methods developed at Task 1 for both sets of data (drivers records for the non-monitoring bins and sensors readings for the monitored bins), and apply the models developed at Task 2 and/or the solution methods developed at Task 3 (depending on the size of the instance) to define a smart collection route plan, which is updated whenever needed; 2) for the non-monitored bins, define the optimal collection frequency and define regular routes for each collection frequency through classical VRP models, and for the monitoring bins, the regular routes will be detoured to collect them when needed. Although monitoring technologies, as volumetric sensors, allow to better understand these systems and to gain insights from the data collected, they are still very pricey. It is then necessary to develop financially more sustainable strategies for integrating sensors into the waste collection activities. For that, in this task, it will be analysed in which circumstances makes sense to have a static sensor embedded in a container to measure its fill level. A decision support model will be proposed, and it must be such that it helps minimizing the investment costs associated with the utilization of the volumetric sensor technology (by monitoring only a reduced number of containers) while maintaining the benefits inherent to its use. Simulations with real data regarding the daily fill levels for all containers inside the pilot-area will be used (already analysed in Task 1). Multi- agent simulation techniques similar to the ones used in [Cos20] are foreseen to be used in this task. The four scenarios are the following: 1. Scenario 1 represents the current solution performed by the waste collection companies so far, i.e., blind collection without collection frequency optimization neither route optimization. For that, the static routes done made the companies in the pilot-area will be analysed: collection frequency, waste collected, kilometres travelled, fill rates of the containers in the moment of the collection (recorded by the drivers), etc. 2. Scenario 2 represents an intermediate solution to assess two effects independently: route optimization and collection frequency optimization, but still in a blind collection context (without any analysis or a priori knowledge of the fill levels). Scenario 2’ represents a blind collection with collection frequency optimization but no route optimization, i.e., the same static routes are performed as in Scenario 1, but with an optimized frequency. Scenario 2’’ represents a blind collection with route optimization but no collection frequency optimization (the same collection frequency as in Scenario 1). To optimize the routes, the models from previous work of [Ram2] will be applied. Scenario 2’’’ represents blind collection with collection frequency and route optimization. This scenario will be the baseline for the benefits assessment of a smart collection versus a blind collection. 3. Scenario 3 represents a smart collection, with a full sensorized network combined with route optimization. For that, the IRP models and solution methods developed at Tasks 2 and 3 will be applied for planning the routes (depending on the size of the real instance both methods can be used, or just the second one for large size instances), and the predictive method from Task 1 will be also use to estimate the fill levels for the days ahead as needed for the IRP. In this scenario, data from the sensors will be simulated based on real data, as said before. 4. Scenario 4, similar to scenario 3 but with real-time information obtained from a sample of containers. In this case, the decision models developed at Task 4 are applied to decide on which containers should be monitored with static sensors. The two strategies devised for Task 4 will be tested here. For the remaining waste bins, the other two monitoring approaches will be considered: mobile sensors and visual observations. The benefits will be assessed in two criteria, as mentioned in Task 2 – Profit and Service Level provided to the population (measured by the number of overflows). The aim is to test the prototype tool in a real environment. While in Task 5 the developed models were tested in a simulated environment, this task aims to test them in a real environment – at ERSUC. The testbed is planned to be performed between April to December in order to test the system at different times of the year, under different weather conditions and different demand volumes. The same pilot-area will be used, where the models developed at Task 4 are applied to decide the static sensor placement in that pilot-area (if the same pilot-area is used, the result was already obtained at Task 4); then, those sensors will be actually installed (we are estimating to install 75 sensors), and the remaining bins are monitored with mobile sensors or visual observations (depending on the results from the previous task). Then, the prototype of the smart waste collection planning tool will be used to inform the company of the collection routes to perform in each day. A close relationship with our partner ERSUC is going to be established during this Task, in order to validate and evaluate the routes suggested by our planning tool. The prototype tool represents an output of this research project that can be immediately usable, with impact to society. The resulting prototype tool will be made available free of charge to waste management companies in the framework of collaboration protocols. Later it can be extended to other areas (e.g., supply system of Liquefied Petroleum Gas tanks, where sensors can monitoring LPG levels in customer’s reservoirs and the supply routes be improved in terms of efficiency and service level – prevention of stockouts). This task will be mainly performed by EVOX and UC teams, but all teams will be involved. text: Pessoas / Mês Alocados 0.36 António José Pais Antunes Universidade de Coimbra Descrição This task is of great importance in a 3-year research project, with 7 different entities involved (CEG-IST, INESC-ID, UC, EVOX, University of Bologna, ERSUC and Valorsul). The complexity of the project, the high number of stakeholders involved and the uncertainty naturally involved in a research project demands for a well-defined project management plan. This task aims to plan, organize, coordinate, integrate and control all the remaining tasks, and identify, plan and manage the project risks, so that the project is completed successfully. The principal investigator (PI) Tânia Ramos, who also holds the Project Management Professional (PMP) certification, will be the responsible person of this task, with the help from the co-PI (Pedro Santos), as well as from the task owners. The project will be monitored on a regular basis to track the overall progress in terms of scope, time, cost, and risk management. Scope management will ensure that all the scientific work is done meeting high-quality standards to accomplish the goals of the project and achieve the expected results in terms of indicators. Time management will ensure a timely completion of the project, where the critical path and milestones achievement will be managed carefully. Cost management will ensure that the project will be completed within the approved budget, where the actual costs will be monitored and compared with the budget plan. Risk management will ensure that the project risks are identified and monitored along with the project, and proper mitigation and contingency plans are devised and applied when needed. Potential risks anticipated at this stage are the following (only the critical points are listed): Risk 1. Difficulty or delay in finding the right candidates for the PhD grants Risk 2. The waste company ERSUC drops out, jeopardizing the testbed task Risk 3. Delay in getting real data from the waste management companies Risk 4. Delay in the sub-tasks assigned to the industrial partner EVOX Risk 5. Delay in installing the sensors for the testbed The mitigation measures and the contingency plan for each risk are the following: Risk 1. Early identification of potential candidates among students with whom the research team as frequent contact (all teams members from the universities teach at the second and third cycle). Risk 2. Careful engagement of ERSUC, discussing the intermediate findings (in a high-light fashion) regularly; if the risk identified happens, the other waste company engaged (Valorsul) could serve as a testbed, using a different geographical area than the one that already has sensors installed. Risk 3. Start working with data from previous projects and simulate data based on that. Risk 4. Add one full dedicated resource to execute the sub-tasks assigned to the industrial partner (as self-financing from the company). Risk 5. Start the testbed with a lower number of sensors. A good communication workflow between all team members will help detecting deviations to the plan in an early stage and corrective actions can be implemented in a fast way. Each team owner will guarantee the sharing of information amongst the researchers involved in their respective task. Every month the task’s leaders will send the PI a synthetic overview of each task development with the main highlights, major opportunities and threats according to the work plan. The PI will compile these overview reports, which will be discussed in the team meetings. The team meetings will happen once a month (virtual meetings) and every trimester a presential meeting will occur, in a rotation scheme: CEG-IST (Lisbon) -> University of Coimbra (Coimbra) -> INESC-ID (Lisbon) -> Evox (Castelo Branco). Thus, 12 presential meetings are foressen. The PI will compile these overview reports, which will be discussed in the team meetings. COMMUNICATION WITH THE TEAM MEMBERS: The team will have internal meetings every month (virtual and presential ones). The international consultant Prof. Daniele Vigo will be invited to participate at some of those meetings. Moreover, a shared folder will be created to share the main documentation of the project. A Skype group or a WhatsApp group will be created to facilitate the communication between team members. Questões éticas Existem questões éticas identificadas neste projeto? Não Declarações de ética que considera apropriadas - Fundamentação - Agenda 2030 Enquadramento da candidatura nos OSD da Agenda 2030 ODS 11: Cidades e Comunidades Sustentáveis ODS 9: Indústria, Inovação e Infraestruturas ODS 6: Água Potável e Saneamento Fundamentação The WSmart Route+ project aligns with SDG 11 Sustainable Cities and Communities, SDG 9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, and SDG 6 Clean Water and Sanitation as it studies a new paradigm on smart waste management. Data analytics combined with route optimization are explored to improve waste collection operation supporting the adoption of a smart collection based on dynamic routes as opposed to the traditional blind collection based on static routes. WSmart Route+ objectives and scientific challenges are: 1) the development of a planning tool combining innovative methods to deal with the complexity related with the definition of smart collection routes, considering data provided by sensors (static and mobile) and by driver’s visual observations; 2) the development of innovative models to decide in which containers static sensors should be installed; 3) the development of a cost-benefit analysis comparing the as-is to the to-be situation in real case studies; 4) the validation of the planning tool prototype with a testbed in a real environment. The ultimate goal of this research is to increase resources efficiency and improve the service level provided to the communities (basic sanitation) in waste management systems towards a more sustainable development. WSmart Route+ contributes to SDG 9, namely to target 9.4, through the development of tools that will make the waste collection industry more sustainable, increasing resource-use efficiency. By using our tools, companies will avoid deadhead situations (travelling many kilometres with no (or few) cargo) and low vehicle usage situations, optimizing resources usage and reducing CO2 emissions. The CO2 emissions per unit of value-added indicator (9.4.1) will significantly decrease. Moreover, having more precise information on the amount of waste existing in each waste bin will also contribute to SDG 6, namely, to target 6.b, given that WSmart Route+ will support and strengthen the participation of local communities (municipalities) in improving sanitation management. Waste bins will be visited when justified in terms of hygiene and public health, i.e., waste bins cannot exceed their maximum capacity to avoid the accumulation of waste around the containers. Thus, waste collection routes will be planned considering more "intelligent" criteria, also preventing containers from being collected when they

Principais resultados do projeto que considera relevantes para esta candidatura
The main results relevant for this application are:
Establish a minimum fill level limit to trigger a collection is not a good strategy; even containers with low filling levels can “be worth it” to
be collected [Ram18]
The collection route to be performed today should consider an estimate of the future fill levels [Mor19]
In the real case studied (for one municipality, and one recyclable material), using smart collection strategies can reduce the number of
routes performed in 33%, and reduce the distance travelled in 30% [Mor22]
These represent the basis/foundation of the WSmart Route+ project.

**5. Case Study: Rio Maior, Portugal**

- Area: 272 km², Santarém District, Central Portugal

text:
Review the PhD methodology as an engineering/research implementation
problem and convert it into a reproducible computational workflow for
Rio Maior recyclable waste collection.

The central research problem is that traditional **"blind collection"**
uses fixed schedules and routes despite uncertain and spatially
heterogeneous waste generation.

The computational system must address the main research gaps: -
real-world data are often poorly integrated; - facility location,
inventory planning and routing are usually studied separately; -
deterministic assumptions dominate despite uncertain fill levels; -
sustainability, service reliability and equity are often omitted; - many
models lack real municipal validation.

Implement the research around these questions:

-   **RQ1 --- System Assessment:** What are the spatial, temporal and
    operational characteristics of the current Rio Maior RWC system?
-   **RQ2 --- Performance:** What are the economic, environmental and
    service-performance characteristics of the baseline system?
-   **RQ3 --- Container Location:** Can stochastic/capacitated p-median
    models improve container allocation under uncertain demand?
-   **RQ4 --- Monitoring/Forecasting:** How well can driver
    observations, sensor data and predictive models estimate container
    fill/waste generation?
-   **RQ5 --- Routing:** How much improvement can optimized
    VRP/IRP/SIRP/DIRP approaches achieve relative to current collection
    practice?

The implementation must support:

A. Baseline characterization\
B. Waste-generation/demand modelling\
C. Fill-level forecasting\
D. Facility-location optimization\
E. Stochastic inventory-routing\
F. Daily routing\
G. Scenario/sensitivity analysis\
H. Cost-benefit and environmental evaluation\
I. Real-world validation

Keep the distinction between: - observed empirical results, -
model-generated results, - simulation results, - literature
benchmarks, - expected/target improvements.

Do not report target percentages as achieved results unless they are
reproduced from the supplied Rio Maior data.

Produce modular code, documented assumptions, reproducible experiments
and thesis-ready tables/figures.

Subject: Additional Literature Supporting the Use of Logarithmic Transformation Dear Professor Bigotte, Thank you very much for your valuable question regarding the use of the logarithmic transformation in my regression model. Following your comment, I reviewed the recent literature to better understand and justify this methodological choice. Based on this review, I found that the use of log(1+Y) is well supported both statistically and theoretically in municipal solid waste modeling. The main arguments are summarized below. 1. Improving the normality assumption The study by Araiza-Aguilar et al. (2020) follows an approach very similar to the one adopted in my research. The authors first evaluated the normality of the dependent and explanatory variables using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. They found that municipal solid waste generation, population, population density, and several other variables were not normally distributed. Consequently, they transformed these variables using the natural logarithm before estimating the multiple linear regression model. Their results showed a substantial improvement in normality after the logarithmic transformation, supporting the use of this approach for regression modeling. 2. Linearising exponential relationships The second justification comes from Alhanaqtah (2024). This study explains that municipal solid waste generation frequently follows non-linear or exponential trends with variables such as population, GDP, and household consumption. Therefore, logarithmic and semi-logarithmic regression models are more appropriate because they transform exponential relationships into approximately linear ones, improving model estimation and interpretation. 3. Addressing the statistical characteristics of waste data A recent study by Mwakalinga and Samli (2026) also recognises that municipal solid waste data are characterized by positive skewness, spatial dependence and heteroscedasticity. Instead of using a logarithmic transformation, the authors employed a Spatial Lag Gamma Generalised Linear Model because of the spatial nature of their data. Nevertheless, the study confirms that waste generation data rarely satisfy the assumptions of simple linear regression without an appropriate statistical treatment. 4. Theoretical support from urban scaling theory Finally, Lu et al. (Worldwide Scaling of Waste Generation in Urban Systems) demonstrate that municipal solid waste generation follows a power-law relationship with city population. The general relationship is expressed as Y=αPβ which becomes linear after taking logarithms log(Y)=log(α)+βlog(P) This provides a theoretical justification for analyzing waste generation in logarithmic space, since it converts non-linear scaling relationships into linear regression models that are easier to estimate and interpret. Why I used log(1+Y) Considering these studies together, the logarithmic transformation in my research was adopted for four complementary reasons: to improve the normality assumption of the regression model; to linearise potentially exponential relationships between waste generation and explanatory variables; to reduce the influence of skewness and heteroscedasticity commonly observed in waste generation data; and to retain observations with zero waste generation, since log(0) is undefined whereas log(1+0)=0. Therefore, the use of log(1+Y) in my model was not an arbitrary mathematical choice. Rather, it was a methodological decision supported by previous empirical studies and by the statistical characteristics of municipal solid waste generation data. 2. Why was Distance to CBD included? The inclusion of Distance to CBD is also supported by recent literature. From an urban planning perspective, the Central Business District (CBD) represents the concentration of commercial activities, services, employment opportunities, accessibility and urban intensity. Consequently, the distance from the CBD acts as a proxy for several spatial characteristics influencing waste generation. In particular, Golafshani et al. (2026) identified Population, Distance to CBD, and Land Area as the three most influential predictors of municipal solid waste generation using SHAP explainable AI analysis. Their findings indicate that urban form and spatial structure play a significant role in explaining variations in waste generation. شاخص موران (Moran’s I) معیاری برای سنجش خودهمبستگی فضایی (Spatial Autocorrelation) است. این شاخص بررسی می‌کند که آیا مقادیر یک متغیر در یک مکان با مقادیر همان متغیر در مکان‌های مجاور ارتباط دارد یا خیر؛ بنابراین، خودهمبستگی فضایی حالت خاصی از همبستگی است که در آن داده‌ها با خودشان در طول زمان یا مکان مقایسه می‌شوند. [1, 2, 3]

تفاوت همبستگی و خودهمبستگی فضایی

همبستگی (Correlation): رابطه بین دو متغیر مختلف (\(X\) و \(Y\)) را در یک نقطه یا مجموعه داده می‌سنجد.

خودهمبستگی (Autocorrelation): رابطه یک متغیر با خودش در زمان‌های مختلف (خودهمبستگی سری زمانی) یا مکان‌های مختلف (خودهمبستگی فضایی) را بررسی می‌کند.

نقش شاخص موران

خودهمبستگی فضایی مثبت: مقادیر مشابه در کنار هم قرار دارند و الگوی توزیع خوشه‌ای تشکیل می‌شود (نزدیک به ۱+).

خودهمبستگی فضایی منفی: مقادیر متضاد در کنار هم قرار دارند و الگوی توزیع پراکنده یا شطرنجی است (نزدیک به ۱-).

عدم خودهمبستگی: توزیع داده‌ها در فضا کاملاً تصادفی است (نزدیک به صفر). [1, 2, 3]

اگر می‌خواهید بیشتر بدانید، بگویید:

آیا مایل به بررسی تفاوت موران جهانی (Global) و موران محلی (Local) هستید؟

یا نیاز به فرمول ریاضی و نحوه محاسبه آن دارید؟

Analysis of Recyclables Waste Collection Infrastructure and Operations: Application to a Portuguese Municipality”. منطق کلی رساله هسته اصلی رساله این است که ابتدا سیستم موجود Recyclables Waste Collection (RWC) در Rio Maior به‌طور کامل شناخته شود و سپس بخش‌های مختلف آن یکی‌یکی ارزیابی و بهینه‌سازی شوند. هدف کلی صراحتاً «توسعه یک روش‌شناسی برای مشخصه‌سازی زیرساخت و عملیات RWC و شناسایی Maior و ساختار رساله معرفی می‌شوند. نکته مهم این است که General Objective در فایل مشخص شده، اما Specific Objectives هنوز واقعاً نوشته نشده‌اند؛ فقط عبارت “Specific objectives” آمده است. بنابراین یکی سمت یک ارزیابی اقتصادی و اجتماعی گسترش می‌دهد. هدف این است که تمام مؤلفه‌های هزینه و منفعت زیرساخت و عملیات RWC شناسایی و برای Rio Maior تخمین زده شوند. سند صراحتاً تأکید می‌کند که باید بین social costs/benefits و company costs/benefits تمایز ایجاد شود. بنابراین تحلیل صرفاً محدود به هزینه سوخت، خودرو و نیروی انسانی نیست؛ منطق فصل این است که دیدگاه شرکت و جامعه از یکدیگر جدا شوند. اما در این فایل هنوز روش کمی Cost–Benefit Analysis، شاخص‌ها، دوره تحلیل، نرخ تنزیل یا نحوه monetization منافع اجتماعی تعیین نشده است. این بخش در مقایسه با فصل 4 هنوز روش‌شناسی کمتری دارد. فصل 4 — Container Location فصل چهارم یکی از روشن‌ترین فصل‌های تحقیق از نظر Research Question → Method است. سؤال اصلی این است که: آیا توزیع فضایی فعلی مخازن با توجه به توزیع جمعیت، ویژگی‌های جمعیت، فعالیت‌های اقتصادی و میزان واقعی مواد بازیافتی تولیدشده، بهترین توزیع ممکن است؟ و پاسخ روش‌شناختی مشخص شده است: p-median type stochastic model. این فصل بنابراین احتمالاً یکی از اصلی‌ترین contributions کمی رساله خواهد بود. استفاده از عبارت stochastic نیز مهم است؛ یعنی طرح اولیه فقط یک p-median قطعی ساده را در نظر ندارد و قرار است عدم‌قطعیت، احتمالاً در تقاضا یا میزان تولید مواد بازیافتی، وارد مدل شود. اما فایل هنوز مشخص نمی‌کند چه متغیری stochastic خواهد بود، سناریوها چگونه تعریف می‌شوند، تابع هدف دقیق چیست و چه constraints وارد مدل می‌شوند. این‌ها باید در توسعه فصل مشخص شوند. فصل 5 — Driver-based vs. Sensor-based Fill Level این فصل از نظر داده و نوآوری بسیار جالب است، زیرا دو منبع اطلاعاتی متفاوت را مقایسه می‌کند: Driver estimates در مقابل Sensor measurements. دو سؤال اصلی تعریف شده است: اول اینکه برآورد سطح پرشدگی توسط رانندگان چه تفاوتی با داده سنسورها دارد، و دوم اینکه این تفاوت‌ها چه تأثیری بر short-term fill-level forecasts خواهند داشت. برای پاسخ، قرار است تعدادی مخزن «نماینده» انتخاب شوند و تحلیل
